performers: Hochschulsymphonieorchester, University of Music and Theatre Munich; Marcus Bosch, conductor
intro: A long cello melody rises above trembling violins and travels through the orchestra. In this live Munich performance under Marcus Bosch, Bruckner saves the timpani for the closing pages: one sustained roll beneath an immense E-major farewell.

sections.label: A · Cellos and horn over trembling violins
sections.mNote: The long E-major melody rises from the cello’s low register

sections.label: B · Oboe and clarinet sing together
sections.mNote: The second theme begins quietly, marked Ruhig

sections.label: C · Strings step out in octaves
sections.mNote: Shorter phrases and repeated bass notes set a walking pace

sections.label: D · Winds alone with soft brass
sections.mNote: The strings stop; flute, oboe and clarinet exchange phrases

sections.label: Dev · Cellos begin again softly
sections.mNote: Flute and bassoons hold notes above the returning cello figure

sections.label: Dev · Flute fragments and moving basses
sections.mNote: Ruhig brings a quieter exchange of short phrases

sections.label: Dev · The theme overturned in C minor
sections.mNote: Winds descend in canon above emphatic brass and string chords

sections.label: Link · Quiet phrases climb towards E major
sections.mNote: Oboe, clarinet and bassoon continue after the brass fall silent

sections.label: A′ · The cello tune meets its reflection
sections.mNote: Ascending and descending versions of the melody sound together

sections.label: D′ · Winds trade phrases above moving strings
sections.mNote: Ruhig returns before the last full-orchestra crescendo

sections.label: Coda · The timpani’s long E
sections.mNote: The drum enters for the first time, very softly

cues.title: The cello’s long climb
cues.text: Cellos and a solo horn rise through E major above trembling violins. Violas join the melody, then a clarinet. The line keeps growing as each new instrument enters; Bruckner lets a single breath of melody occupy almost the whole opening page.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), I, printed p. 5. Opening instrumentation also described by the Berlin Philharmonic: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/symphony-no-7-in-e-major/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A candle beside the bed
cues.text: Bruckner tells Hans Richter that the melody comes to him in a dream. His old mentor Ignaz Dorn plays it on a viola and promises him success. Bruckner wakes, lights a candle and writes the tune down.
cues.evidence: Bruckner’s recollection, related to Hans Richter; date of the conversation unspecified. Thomas May, St. Louis Symphony programme note, 9 February 2020: https://slso.org/bruckners-seventh/

cues.title: Oboe and clarinet together
cues.text: Oboe and clarinet begin the second theme, marked Ruhig — calm. Beneath their joined voices, the strings keep separate lines moving. This gentle tune has considerable ingenuity hidden inside it: later, the strings turn its melody upside down.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter B, p. 7. The Munich analysis illustrates the second group’s counterpoint and subsequent melodic inversion: https://openmusic.academy/docs/bmwvSwGA9xQFLhfL4GJukj/anton-bruckner-sinfonie-nr7-e-dur-wab-107
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A walk in octaves
cues.text: The violins step forward in octaves while the basses repeat short notes. Bruckner marks the violin line immer hervortretend — always prominent. Its compact phrases give this third theme a brisker gait than the long melodies before it.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter D, p. 9. Third-theme character also described in the Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cellos under held wind notes
cues.text: The cellos resume the opening figure quietly beneath sustained flute and bassoon notes. Soon clarinet, bassoon and horn take it apart. A melody that began as one enormous line becomes a conversation in smaller phrases.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letters I–K, pp. 14–15; cello figure and sustained winds at I, exchanges at K.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The melody falls in canon
cues.text: The opening melody turns upside down in C minor. Woodwind entries chase one another downwards, while brass and strings strike the chords beneath them. Bruckner restores Tempo I and gives the quiet development an abrupt, formidable interruption.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter M, pp. 16–17. Inversion, C minor and canonic treatment described by the Hungarian National Philharmonic: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The cello meets its reflection
cues.text: The opening cello tune returns with horn and trumpet. Above it, flute and first violins play its descending reflection. Two shapes of the same melody fit together, one climbing as the other falls.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter O, p. 19. The simultaneous inversion is illustrated in the Munich analysis: https://openmusic.academy/docs/bmwvSwGA9xQFLhfL4GJukj/anton-bruckner-sinfonie-nr7-e-dur-wab-107
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nikisch brings it to Leipzig
cues.text: On 30 December 1884, Arthur Nikisch conducts the premiere with the Gewandhaus Orchestra in Leipzig’s Neues Theater. Liszt and excerpts from Wagner’s Götterdämmerung share the programme. At sixty, Bruckner has the great public success his symphonies have long been denied.
cues.evidence: Premiere date, venue, performers and programme: Berlin Philharmonic programme note, https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/symphony-no-7-in-e-major/. Bruckner was born in September 1824.

cues.title: The timpani finally enter
cues.text: The timpani begin a soft roll on E. They have been silent throughout the movement. Double basses hold the same note while clarinets, oboe and flute climb above them; Bruckner marks the passage sehr feierlich — very solemn.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter W, p. 28. The first timpani entry and prolonged roll are also identified by the Hungarian National Philharmonic: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One chord, more and more players
cues.text: E major holds beneath flowing violin figures and broad wind phrases. Trombones, tuba and timpani sustain the bass while the other instruments join the climb. The instruction begins “very calm”, then asks for a little more speed, gradually.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter X, pp. 29–32: Sehr ruhig; nach und nach etwas schneller, E pedal and orchestration.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Oboe and clarinet take over
transitions.from: A · Cellos and horn over trembling violins
transitions.to: B · Oboe and clarinet sing together
transitions.how: The first great crescendo subsides into quiet strings. At B, marked Ruhig, oboe and clarinet begin the new tune together. Horn and trumpet supply soft held notes while the violins and violas weave shorter phrases beneath the wind melody.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), I, letter B, p. 7.

transitions.title: The violins take a brisker step
transitions.from: B · Oboe and clarinet sing together
transitions.to: C · Strings step out in octaves
transitions.how: Flowing woodwind figures lead to the third theme. The violins begin it in octaves, marked immer hervortretend, above repeated bass notes and sustained lower-string chords. A soft horn note bridges the entrance; the winds return as the string phrase grows.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter D and preceding bars, p. 9.

transitions.title: The strings leave the winds alone
transitions.from: C · Strings step out in octaves
transitions.to: D · Winds alone with soft brass
transitions.how: The orchestra’s forceful closing phrases dwindle to quiet strings. At H, Ruhig, the strings stop altogether. Flute, oboe and clarinet trade phrases above soft horn and trombone notes, leaving the double basses silent too.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter H and preceding bars, p. 14.

transitions.title: Cellos return beneath held winds
transitions.from: D · Winds alone with soft brass
transitions.how: The woodwind passage slows under a ritardando. At I, a tempo, the cellos begin a rising figure beneath sustained flute and bassoon notes. Violas and basses return with held notes, followed by quiet violin chords and an oboe phrase.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter I, p. 14.

transitions.title: Flute and basses divide the phrase
transitions.to: Dev · Flute fragments and moving basses
transitions.how: The brass crescendo gives way to exchanges among flute and strings. At L, marked Ruhig, the flute plays a short, detached phrase while cellos and basses begin a continuous line below it. Violins answer, then clarinet joins the exchange.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letters K–L, pp. 15–16.

transitions.title: A descending theme strikes in C minor
transitions.from: Dev · Flute fragments and moving basses
transitions.to: Dev · The theme overturned in C minor
transitions.how: Soft flute phrases and held strings lead directly into M, Tempo I. The woodwinds begin the opening theme upside down in C minor, with bassoons following in canon. Horns, trumpets and low brass add emphatic rhythms against the strings’ heavy chords.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter M, pp. 16–17; C-minor inversion also described by the Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note.

transitions.title: Oboe and clarinet emerge from the brass
transitions.from: Dev · The theme overturned in C minor
transitions.to: Link · Quiet phrases climb towards E major
transitions.how: The C-minor tutti ends. At N, oboe, clarinet and bassoon resume softly with horn and strings; trumpets and low brass stop. These interwoven phrases carry the music through D and E♭ towards the returning E-major melody.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter N, pp. 17–19. Tonal route: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/

transitions.title: The cello tune returns beneath its inversion
transitions.from: Link · Quiet phrases climb towards E major
transitions.to: A′ · The cello tune meets its reflection
transitions.how: At O, the cellos bring back the E-major opening tune, joined by horn and then trumpet. Flute and first violins descend above it with the tune’s inversion. Second violins and violas provide quiet tremolo chords; the basses remain silent.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter O, p. 19. Counterpoint illustrated in the Munich analysis cited above.

transitions.title: Short wind phrases replace the broad chords
transitions.from: A′ · The cello tune meets its reflection
transitions.to: D′ · Winds trade phrases above moving strings
transitions.how: The broad orchestral phrases give way to T, Ruhig. Flutes and oboes place short phrases above a moving clarinet line. Strings answer and overlap them, with a soft horn joining between entries. The repeated calm marking recalls the exposition’s wind-led close.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter T, p. 25, compared with H, p. 14.

transitions.title: A soft drum roll on E
transitions.from: D′ · Winds trade phrases above moving strings
transitions.how: After the recapitulation’s closing climax, W begins sehr feierlich. The timpani enter for the first time, rolling softly on E above a held double-bass E. Clarinet starts the rising wind line; cellos and violas move beneath it while violins hold quiet chords.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, I, letter W, p. 28.

source.title: Bruckner, Symphony No. 7, full score (Vienna: A. J. Gutmann, 1885, plate A.J.G. 576; first edition)
source.locator: I. Allegro moderato, printed pp. 5–32; opening melody, letters B, G–I, M–P and W–X.

timeline.note: Tremolo violins; the theme rises in the cellos with a solo horn.
A clarinet and the violas take up the theme; basses join in a crescendo.
The theme returns with flutes, oboes, clarinets and bassoons added.
Trombones and tuba join the crescendo to the first climax.
After the climax the sound thins to oboes, clarinets, horns and strings.
The ruhig second group: oboes and clarinets sing over thinner strings.
The exposition’s final wave; brass repeat short rhythmic notes at its peak.
The ruhig close: flute, oboe and clarinet over soft trombones and horns; strings silent.
Winds play the inverted theme in C minor, with brass rhythms and heavy string chords.
After the tutti, soft woodwind, horn and string phrases.
Cellos, horn and trumpet rise against the descending melody in flute and first violins.
Very soft tremolo strings support brief woodwind phrases.
The whole orchestra builds to the last fortissimo climax before the coda.
The coda: a soft timpani roll, their first entry, beneath a woodwind line and strings.
First violins run above repeated string chords, held low brass and the continuing timpani roll.
The whole orchestra drives to the final E major chord.

composer.epithet: He spent half his life learning his trade, then wrote symphonies in which a horn call can grow into a wall of brass.
facts: St Florian; counterpoint with Simon Sechter, 1855–61; composition with Otto Kitzler, 1861–63
Organist at St Florian and Linz; Vienna Conservatory from 1868; university lecturer from 1875
Nine numbered symphonies, two outside the sequence; masses, motets and secular choral music
The Seventh Symphony, Leipzig, 30 December 1884; Arthur Nikisch conducting
composer.background:
On 16 December 1877 Bruckner stood before the Vienna Philharmonic to conduct his Third Symphony. Johann Herbeck, who had intended to conduct it, had died in October. The audience began to leave. Among the supporters who stayed was the seventeen-year-old Mahler, who helped turn the enormous score into a piano duet. Bruckner was fifty-three, a conservatory professor and an internationally admired organist. In the concert hall he was still having to introduce himself.

He was born in Ansfelden, near Linz, where his father taught school and played church music. After his father died in 1837, his mother took him to the Augustinian abbey of St Florian as a choirboy. He learned the organ, trained as a teacher and worked in the villages of Windhaag and Kronstorf. In Windhaag he also played the fiddle for dancing. The heavy-footed country dances in his scherzos had passed through his hands long before he wrote for an orchestra.
